lesson.title: No Lifting the Pencil: Continuous Functions
lesson.summary: Continuous functions can be traced without gaps or jumps because every real number in an interval is a valid input.
lesson.body:
A continuous function is a function whose graph can be traced from start to finish without ever lifting your pencil off the paper: no gaps, no holes, and no sudden jumps. Unlike a discrete function, whose domain is limited to separated values like the whole numbers, a continuous function is typically defined over an entire interval of real numbers, which means every value in that interval, including all the fractions and decimals packed between any two numbers, is a valid input.

Continuous functions describe quantities that can change smoothly through every in-between value, not just whole-number steps. Time, distance, temperature, and height are classic examples: a car does not skip over 1.5 hours on its way from hour 1 to hour 2, and a thermometer does not jump straight from 70 degrees to 71 degrees without passing through 70.3, 70.5, and 70.9 along the way.

Consider a car traveling at a constant speed of 55 miles per hour. The distance function is d(t) = 55t, where t is the time in hours since the trip began, and t can be any nonnegative real number, not just whole hours. Evaluate a few inputs: d(1) = 55, d(1.5) = 82.5, and d(2) = 110. Because every real number of hours between 0 and the end of the trip is a legitimate input with a sensible output, the graph of d(t) = 55t is an unbroken ray starting at the origin, and you could trace it with a pencil from (0, 0) onward without ever picking the pencil up.

Compare that smooth ray to a function with a sudden jump, such as a flat shipping fee that charges 5 dollars for any package up to 2 pounds and then jumps immediately to 11 dollars for anything just over 2 pounds. At the exact boundary near 2 pounds, the output leaps from 5 to 11 with no in-between values ever appearing, so that graph cannot be traced without lifting the pencil right at the jump. Functions built this way, out of connected pieces that do not always meet up smoothly, are the subject of the next chapter on piecewise functions, and they are the clearest everyday examples of functions that are not continuous.

Not every continuous function needs an unlimited domain to make sense, and that is part of what distinguishes it from many discrete examples. The height of a football after it is thrown, modeled by a quadratic function like h(t) = -16t^2 + 48t, is continuous over the whole flight because the ball passes through every height between the ground and its peak, never skipping any value. Even though the ball is only in the air for a few seconds, within that short window every real number of seconds, and every real number of feet in height, is a legitimate part of the function's behavior.

Knowing whether a function is continuous tells you a great deal before you even look closely at its formula: you can expect its graph to be a single unbroken curve, you can trust that values between any two known outputs are also achievable, and you can safely read the graph by following the line rather than searching for isolated dots. That expectation is exactly what breaks down once jumps, breaks, or restricted domains enter the picture.
